stories.summary: Amit and about fifteen friends took a bus through Mysore and Mangalore on a food trip, with destinations on an Excel sheet and roughly eight meals a day. Within a five-kilometer radius of Mangalore alone, they tried five different kinds of biryani, each authentic to the place and arisen in different ways from the same little area.
stories.insight: A small concrete demonstration that culture is a kichri — even within a five-kilometre stretch of one Indian region, the 'authentic' is itself the layered residue of trade. Globalisation is not abstract; it lives on your plate, multiple times in the same town.

stories.topic: The 1100-Rupee Casio That Could Not Have Existed
stories.summary: Ajay holds up his Casio wristwatch, paid for with all of 1100 rupees, and notes it could not have been done without the ability to buy things from people overseas. The privilege of trade, he argues, is not exporting to amass gold — it is importing the wonders of the whole world for the lives of ordinary people.
stories.insight: A tiny everyday object refutes mercantilism. Exports are merely the means; the end is the citizen's life enhanced by what they can buy. Once you flip the frame from 'government's gold' to 'people's lives,' the export obsession dissolves.

stories.topic: Young Indian Entrepreneurs Were Rent-Seekers, Not Profit-Seekers
stories.summary: In Amit's young years, whenever he met someone who wanted to start a business, he was repeatedly shocked at how openly extractive their thinking was — how to use proximity to the state, monopoly, or regulation to make money rather than how to create value for a customer. Bhagwati had observed the same contrast: in China people's mentality was profit-seeking, in India it was rent-seeking.
stories.insight: A closed economy doesn't just slow growth — it deforms the moral imagination of an entire entrepreneurial generation. When the levers to prosperity sit with the state, the natural ambition becomes capturing the state, not serving the customer. Opening trade rewires what 'making money' even means.

stories.summary: Mid-recording, Ajay keeps looking at Amit and saying 'Amit said, Amit said.' Amit interrupts to remind him to look at the camera and say 'Amit said,' or look at Amit and say 'as you said' — either of which would suitably flatter Amit by quoting him to himself.
stories.insight: A small piece of self-aware podcast craft. Direct address to the audience versus direct address to the co-host are different rhetorical moves; getting them right is part of producing a show that will be a 'resource for the future.'

stories.topic: Sowell's 1929 Numbers vs. The Popular Story of the Great Depression
stories.summary: In the popular telling, the October 1929 stock market crash caused the Great Depression. Thomas Sowell's data tells a different story: unemployment peaked at 9% shortly after the crash and was already declining to 6.3% by June 1930. Then President Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley tariffs to 'lift employment' by protecting domestic industry; within five months unemployment shot back above 10% and stayed double-digit for the rest of the decade.
stories.insight: What turned a recession into a Depression was not the crash but the policy response — a textbook case of mercantilist intuition causing the catastrophe it was supposed to prevent. The story illustrates Bastiat's seen-vs-unseen: the 'protected' jobs were visible, the trade-war collapse was not.

stories.topic: The Smoot-Hawley Line Runs to World War II
stories.summary: Smoot-Hawley triggered global reciprocal tariffs; world trade collapsed by roughly 66% from 1929 to 1933. Economic hardship hollowed out the political centre, opening room for nationalist and communist extremism. When the global trading system stopped delivering resources, leaders turned to conquest — Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931, Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, and Hitler's Lebensraum doctrine recast war as the substitute for trade Germany felt locked out of.
stories.insight: Trade is not just an economic mechanism — it is the alternative to war. When you make voluntary exchange impossible, leaders default to taking by force what they can no longer buy. There is a direct line from a tariff bill in Washington to the eastern front. Norman Angell's 1909 'too intertwined to fight' was wrong because the intertwining was reversed by policy, not preserved.

stories.topic: The Loss of First-Wave Globalisation Innocence
stories.summary: Amit quotes Keynes from The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919): 'In 1914, the inhabitant of London could order by telephone, sipping his morning tea, the various products of the whole earth, and reasonably expect their early delivery at his doorstep.' That first wave of globalisation — built on Smith and Ricardo's victories — felt like a settled human achievement. World War I shattered it, made the world cynical, and led to the disastrous interwar decades.
stories.insight: Globalisation, like democracy, is not a one-way ratchet. The pre-1914 world was, by some measures, more economically integrated than ours — and it came apart. The lesson Amit draws: people who think the current global order is a 'done deal' are repeating Norman Angell's 1909 mistake.

stories.topic: Ricardo's Cloth and Wine — Trade Even When You're Worse At Everything
stories.summary: David Ricardo's original example: Portugal may be better than England at both making cloth and making wine. Intuition says Portugal should do both; comparative advantage says no. Portugal should specialise in whichever it is *most* superior at — say wine — and import cloth from England. The man-hours saved on cloth, redirected into wine, leave both countries with more of both. Specialisation by ratio, not by absolute skill, is the engine.
stories.insight: A profound, counter-intuitive idea: a country can be bad at *everything* and still gain from trade, because what matters is the ratio of relative superiority, not the absolute level. India's poverty is no impediment to participating in world trade — only the failure to specialise is.

stories.topic: Why Virat Kohli Should Not Drive Himself
stories.summary: Suppose Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma are the best drivers in Bombay — better than any chauffeur. Should they drive themselves to work? No. Their time is better spent on cricket prep or reading scripts; even an inferior driver frees up the higher-value activity. Comparative advantage applies even when you are absolutely better at the task.
stories.insight: The Kohli-Sharma example translates Ricardo into one's own life. The question is never 'am I better than the other person at this?' but 'is this where my time creates the most value?' The same logic explains why a country shouldn't try to make everything itself.

recommendations.item: Basic Economics
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: Sowell's signature introduction to economics for the general reader.
recommendations.reason: Amit's pick for learning the basic concepts in simple language. Calls Sowell one of the great thinkers of the 20th century — a towering figure now 94 — and recommends reading all his books.

recommendations.item: Applied Economics
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: Sowell's companion volume showing how economic principles play out in policy and practice.
recommendations.reason: The natural follow-up to Basic Economics for readers who want to see how the same intuitions explain real-world outcomes.

recommendations.item: Economics in One Lesson
recommendations.creator: Henry Hazlitt
recommendations.context: The classic short primer built around Bastiat's seen-vs-unseen lesson.
recommendations.reason: A foundational text for spotting the unseen costs of state interventions like tariffs — exactly the trap Hoover and Trump fall into.

recommendations.item: Timeless Essays on Political Economy
recommendations.creator: Frederic Bastiat
recommendations.context: A collection of Bastiat's essays.
recommendations.reason: Amit recommends 'everything by Frederic Bastiat' as essential for understanding the moral and economic case against intervention.

recommendations.item: In Defense of Globalization
recommendations.creator: Jagdish Bhagwati
recommendations.context: Bhagwati's book-length defence of free trade.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's closing recommendation as the definitive treatment of why globalisation works and where critics misread it.

recommendations.item: The Wealth of Nations
recommendations.creator: Adam Smith
recommendations.context: Smith's 1776 founding text of economics.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Smith the Charles Darwin of economics — the literal starting point. 'The first grand ideas, the clarity, the deep intuitions of economics are all in The Wealth of Nations. Even today it is eerie how much he understood and how much he got right.'

recommendations.item: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
recommendations.creator: Adam Smith
recommendations.context: Smith's earlier work, before The Wealth of Nations.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it a philosophical masterpiece and notes he has a Seen and the Unseen episode on it with Russ Roberts.

recommendations.item: Conversation and Society (Episode 182, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Russ Roberts
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Russ Roberts focused on Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's pointer for listeners who want to dive into Smith's moral philosophy via Roberts.

recommendations.item: The Great Illusion
recommendations.creator: Norman Angell
recommendations.context: Angell's 1909 book arguing that trade interdependence had made war obsolete.
recommendations.reason: Now famous as a cautionary tale: published five years before World War I, it captured the over-confidence of the first wave of globalisation. A reminder that 'incentives are aligned' is not the same as 'incentives will hold.'

recommendations.item: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
recommendations.creator: John Maynard Keynes
recommendations.context: Keynes's 1919 indictment of the Versailles Treaty.
recommendations.reason: Source of the iconic 1914 Londoner-with-tea passage Amit quotes — the most vivid single image of how integrated the pre-WWI world economy was, and what was lost.

recommendations.item: Thomas Sowell Interviewed by Peter Robinson
recommendations.creator: Peter Robinson with Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: A recent (April 2025) Hoover Institution interview where 94-year-old Sowell speaks on Trump's tariffs.
recommendations.reason: Sowell explicitly returns to his decades-old warnings about Smoot-Hawley and says it is 'the same damn thing happening again' — directly relevant to the current moment.

recommendations.item: The Great Redistribution
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column applying his 'every state intervention redistributes wealth from poor to rich' argument.
recommendations.reason: Self-recommended for the deeper version of Verma's Law — the claim that tariffs and similar interventions redistribute wealth from many poor consumers to one rich rent-seeker.

recommendations.item: A Trade Deficit With a Babysitter
recommendations.creator: Tim Harford
recommendations.context: Harford's essay using the parent-babysitter relationship to illustrate trade deficits.
recommendations.reason: Amit's go-to debunking of the 'trade deficit equals loss' fallacy — Harford runs a permanent deficit with his babysitter and both parties are perfectly happy.

recommendations.item: I, Pencil
recommendations.creator: Leonard Read
recommendations.context: Read's first-person essay narrated by a humble pencil.
recommendations.reason: The classic illustration of price-coordinated specialisation: a single pencil is the product of perhaps forty countries cooperating without any central planner, organised only by prices. Used here as the proof that hyper-specialisation, not self-sufficiency, is what makes good things cheap.

recommendations.item: The Double 'Thank You' Moment
recommendations.creator: John Stossel
recommendations.context: Stossel's framing of the cafe transaction.
recommendations.reason: Source of the show's recurring shorthand for positive-sum exchange: customer says thank you for the coffee, barista says thank you for the money. Both walked away better off — that is what every voluntary trade is.

recommendations.item: India's Problem Is Poverty, Not Inequality
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column distinguishing the two concepts.
recommendations.reason: Re-recommended here to underline the central counterintuitive finding of the globalisation era — between 1988 and 2013 global extreme poverty fell from 35% to 10% even as within-country inequality often rose. Different problems, different solutions.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on Indian economic policymaking.
recommendations.reason: The standing reference for Ajay's frameworks — including the rent-seeking vs profit-seeking distinction and the political-economy reasons closed economies breed elite conflict.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's earlier episode framing Indian history as a freedom-and-economic-success story.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's recommended companion piece — the founding story of India's opening up, critically linked to embracing globalisation.

recommendations.item: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A deep dive into the 1991 liberalisation.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's pointer for listeners born after 1991 who need to know the founding story of where Indian success came from.

recommendations.item: Nothing Is Indian! Everything Is Indian! (Episode 12, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on how Indian culture is itself the product of trade.
recommendations.reason: Source of the argument that everything we consider quintessentially Indian — clothes, food, languages — actually came from somewhere else and is a melding of influences. No culture is sui generis.

recommendations.item: Pushpesh Pant Feasts on the Buffet of Life (Episode 326, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pushpesh Pant
recommendations.context: Amit's deep dive with the food historian Pushpesh Pant.

recommendations.item: The Indianness of Indian Food (Episode 95, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Doctor
recommendations.context: Amit's earlier Seen and the Unseen episode with Vikram Doctor.

recommendations.item: A Brief History of Globalization
recommendations.creator: Peter Vanham
recommendations.context: Peter Vanham's World Economic Forum overview of how globalization has evolved.
recommendations.reason: Amit reads from this piece on the post-Columbian-Exchange transformation of the global diet ('Imagine Italian cuisine without tomatoes...'). Useful as a one-page tour of the four phases.

recommendations.item: The Art of Podcasting (Episode 49, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode on Indian education.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode on what the state is and does.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

recommendations.context: EIE episode on Lant Pritchett's development findings.

recommendations.item: The Reformers (Episode 28, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on the architects of India's 1991 liberalisation.
recommendations.reason: Companion to the 1991 reforms episode — the people behind the policy turn that drove the largest poverty reduction in Indian history.

recommendations.item: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on internationalisation as a discipline for firms.
recommendations.reason: Source of Ajay's argument that competing globally forces firms to import best practices, lift standards, and avoid the ossification of insulated companies.

core_ideas.concept: Trade Is Always a Positive-Sum Game (The Double Thank You Moment)
core_ideas.explanation: Every voluntary transaction makes both parties better off — buyer values the coffee more than the money, seller values the money more than the coffee. Hence the 'double thank you' that bookends a cafe purchase. Mercantilist and Trumpian rhetoric treats trade as a profit-and-loss balance sheet between countries; first-principles reasoning shows trade is never about winners and losers, only about both sides being better off than before. The crucial qualifier is *voluntary*: colonial extraction is not a counter-example because those exchanges were not voluntary.
core_ideas.quote: Every voluntary action between two consenting adults is always a positive sum game. It is a double thank you moment.

core_ideas.explanation: Even if Portugal is better than England at *both* wine and cloth, both gain by Portugal specialising in whichever it is most superior at and importing the other. What matters is the ratio of relative superiority, not absolute skill. This means a country bad at almost everything still gains from trade — and an individual better than her chauffeur at driving still gains from outsourcing the drive. The deep counterintuitive lesson: there is no precondition of being 'good at things' to participate in international trade.
core_ideas.quote: It doesn't matter that you are good at something. There is nothing that you are particularly good at... we will still be better off trading because the ratio of how much you are superior to me will vary.

core_ideas.concept: Imports, Not Exports, Are the Privilege
core_ideas.explanation: Mercantilism inverts the goal: it treats exports as good (gold flows in) and imports as bad (gold flows out). The first-principles view is the opposite: 'There's no fun in exporting, the real fun is in importing.' We export *in order* to acquire foreign exchange with which to import the wonders of the world. The 1100-rupee Casio is the proof. The 'export obsession' typically reflects governments' interests (gold in the treasury, public choice incentives), not the citizens' (cheap, varied goods).
core_ideas.quote: The privilege is not money sitting with some government, it is that the lives of the people are enhanced — and it comes from exporting as a means to importing.

core_ideas.concept: Tariffs Redistribute Wealth From Your Own Poor to Your Own Rich (Verma's Law)
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's coined formulation: every interference in free markets redistributes wealth from the poor to the rich. Tariffs are the cleanest example. A 100-rupee Chinese widget plus a 20-rupee tariff forces consumers to buy the 110-rupee local equivalent. The 10 extra rupees that would have circulated in many double-thank-you transactions now flow to one protected domestic producer. Plus a separate price effect: domestic shirt-makers, freed of foreign competition at 500, raise their own price to 550. Tariffs are paid by your own consumers — twice.
core_ideas.quote: Every interference in free markets redistributes wealth from the poor to the rich, and tariffs are an indisputable example of this.

core_ideas.concept: A Trade Deficit Is an Accounting Identity, Not a Loss
core_ideas.explanation: Across the balance of payments, total dollars purchased must equal total dollars sold — same as any market clears. Capital activities (foreign investment, asset purchases) and trade activities (imports, exports) sum to zero. If capital is flowing into a country (a sign of investor confidence), that country *must* run a trade deficit by accounting necessity. A trade deficit therefore tells you nothing about national well-being on its own. Tim Harford runs a permanent trade deficit with his babysitter; both are happy. The word 'deficit' carries an unrelated emotional charge from fiscal contexts.
core_ideas.quote: It is an accounting fact that if you have capital coming into a country, you will always have a deficit on the trade account.

core_ideas.concept: Tariffs Hurt The Local Industries They Pretend to Protect
core_ideas.explanation: Two mechanisms. First, around half of imports into the US are *inputs* used by local manufacturers — so a tariff is a tax on domestic production, not just on foreign goods. Second, insulated firms ossify: when they compete only for political influence rather than against the world's best, they don't import best practices, raise standards, or expand scope. India's ambassador and Premier Padmini cars, frozen by decades of trade barriers, are the example: protection produced stagnation, not greatness.
core_ideas.quote: A company that has to compete with global competitors will import best practices, lift its standards, do better, and just become a better company.

core_ideas.concept: Globalisation Reduces Elite Conflict Inside a Country
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's elaboration on Bhagwati-Srinivasan-Krueger. In a closed economy, domestic elites view the economy as a finite landscape and fight each other for slices of a fixed pie — wasteful, knife-in-the-back competition. Open the economy outward and the relevant arena becomes the world; elites can now align around policies that strengthen the country in global competition. Better policy gets done because the game is positive-sum, and overall conflict in the polity goes down.
core_ideas.quote: When you switch over to a globalization orientation, the elite is thinking that the game I'm playing is the world. I'm not playing in this country.

core_ideas.explanation: Bhagwati's observation: in China people's mentality is profit-seeking — making money by creating value for someone else in a double-thank-you transaction. In India for decades it was rent-seeking — making money by exploiting state-granted monopolies, tariffs, entry barriers. Closed economies *manufacture* the rent-seeking mentality because the levers to prosperity sit with the state. Opening the economy turns the natural ambition outward: serving customers globally rather than capturing the regulator domestically.
core_ideas.quote: Either I am part of the state and I make money that way, or I become a crony for the state and I get the state to do things... that mentality is much more in India because we've had a closed economy for so long.

core_ideas.concept: Culture Is Always a Kichri (No Sui Generis Culture)
core_ideas.explanation: Everything we consider quintessentially Indian — clothes, languages, foods, religions — came from somewhere else. The Columbian Exchange gave India the potato, the chilli, the guava. Stitched clothing came from outside. Buddhism, Christianity, Islam all spread along trade routes (Islam first arrived in Kerala as traders during the Prophet's lifetime, not centuries later with invaders). Globalisation is the *origin* of distinctive cultures, not a threat to them. The North Korean alternative is shallowness, not authenticity.
core_ideas.quote: There is literally nothing that we can do, nothing that we can say, nothing that we can eat, nothing that we can wear, which is not a consequence of globalization.

core_ideas.explanation: A single pencil — and far more so a smartphone — is the product of perhaps forty countries cooperating without any central planner, coordinated only by prices. Designs in Silicon Valley, rare earths from Africa, chips fabricated in Taiwan, assembly in China. No one person on earth can make a pencil from scratch. This price-coordinated hyper-specialisation is *the* mechanism by which complex goods become cheap and good. Trying to do everything domestically guarantees substandard, expensive products.
core_ideas.quote: iPencil is a first person account of a pencil which is made through the actions of people in 40 countries, coordinated only by prices, not by a central planner.

core_ideas.concept: Trade As The Alternative To War
core_ideas.explanation: The clearest geopolitical case for free trade. If Germany, Japan, or Italy in the 1930s could not buy rare earths or wheat through trade, the alternative was 'march in and take them.' Smoot-Hawley collapsed world trade by 66% in three years; within months Japan invaded Manchuria, then Italy Ethiopia, then Hitler's Lebensraum doctrine recast eastward conquest as the substitute for the trading system Germany was locked out of. Trade is not just prosperity — it is the mechanism that makes nationalism and conquest unnecessary.
core_ideas.quote: There is a line that runs from Smoot-Hawley to creating the conditions for the Second World War.

core_ideas.concept: Smoot-Hawley As The Hinge of the Great Depression
core_ideas.explanation: In the popular telling, the October 1929 stock market crash *is* the Great Depression. Sowell's data: unemployment peaked at 9% post-crash, was already declining to 6.3% by June 1930, and the recovery was on track. Hoover then signed Smoot-Hawley to lift employment by protecting domestic industry; reciprocal tariffs from every other country triggered a global trade war; within five months US unemployment shot back above 10% and stayed double-digit through the rest of the decade. The lesson: it was the policy response, not the crash, that turned a recession into a Depression.
core_ideas.quote: By June 1930 unemployment was at 6.3%. Then Hoover signed Smoot-Hawley. Within five months unemployment shoots back up to over 10% and for the rest of the 1930s it is a double digit figure.

core_ideas.concept: Reciprocal Tariffs Are Self-Harm, Not Retaliation
core_ideas.explanation: Joan Robinson: 'Just because other countries put rocks on their harbour doesn't mean we have to put rocks on our harbour.' Because a tariff is a tax on your *own* consumers, retaliating with another tariff doesn't punish the foreign country — it punishes your own people a second time. Amit's stance: India should have zero tariffs across the board on every damn thing, regardless of what anyone else does. Free trade is a unilateral gift to your own citizens; making it conditional on reciprocity is a category error.
core_ideas.quote: It doesn't matter what tariffs other people have. We benefit our own people by taking our tariffs to zero. It's not about the other person, it's about our own people.

core_ideas.concept: Goods vs Services Is a Pre-Internet Distinction
core_ideas.explanation: Many people, including Trump, attach mystical importance to goods — 'real' things you can touch — and disdain services. The distinction is an artefact of a pre-fibre-optic world when international trade in services was technically infeasible. Today services are tradable. A call center, a law firm, a contract draft — all equally legitimate exports. There is no economic reason ball bearings are nobler than call-centre calls; obsessing about manufacturing is fetishising a vintage of trade.
core_ideas.quote: There is no reason to think that a ball bearing is somehow better or superior than a call center call.

core_ideas.concept: The Pritchett Finding (Per Capita GDP Drives All Welfare)
core_ideas.explanation: Lant Pritchett's research, frequently cited on the show: across every human welfare indicator — health, education, longevity, infant mortality, anything — the explanatory factor is per-capita GDP, with roughly 99% correlation. Welfare redistribution explains roughly 1%. The implication: economic growth is not 'one factor among many' for human flourishing — it is essentially the whole game. Free trade and openness are therefore not abstract preferences; they are the most morally consequential policies a poor country can adopt.
core_ideas.quote: There's a 99% correlation between economic growth and any human welfare indicator that you take. And only 1% with welfare redistribution.

core_ideas.concept: 1991-2011: India's Greatest Economic Achievement in 10,000 Years
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framing: the 4x rise of GDP from 1991 to 2011 is the largest economic achievement of India in its entire recorded history. It coincides exactly with two decades of falling trade barriers, falling capital controls, and growing openness to foreign investment. Nitin Pai's rule of thumb (revised on better data): every 1% rise in GDP lifts about 2 million people out of poverty. The cause-and-effect is not coincidental. And critically, this is not a partisan story — Congress kickstarted it under Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh, the BJP under Vajpayee continued it; both parties also reversed it later. It is a freedom story, not a political one.
core_ideas.quote: The greatest ever economic achievement of India in the last 10,000 years was the four-fold gain of GDP that happened from 1991 to 2011.

core_ideas.concept: Pre-1914 Globalisation Was Already Complete — And Then It Wasn't
core_ideas.explanation: Keynes's 1914 Londoner could order any product on earth by telephone and receive it at his doorstep. Norman Angell in 1909 declared war impossible because nations were too economically intertwined. Both were factually correct about their moment — and World War I shattered the entire arrangement, ushering in cynicism, mercantilism, and the interwar collapse. The lesson: globalisation is not a one-way ratchet but a set of policy choices that can be undone. Anyone who thinks today's order is permanent is repeating Angell's mistake.
core_ideas.quote: In 1914 the inhabitant of London could order by telephone, sipping his morning tea, the various products of the whole earth, and reasonably expect their early delivery at his doorstep.

core_ideas.concept: Adam Smith As The Darwin of Economics
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's framing: Smith is to economics what Darwin is to biology — the literal starting point. The Wealth of Nations (1776) gave us, in lay-readable language, the positive-sum nature of trade, specialisation, the division of labour, and the invisible hand. The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) is a philosophical masterpiece in its own right. Smith's articulations sat for decades before Pax Britannica and the 1846 repeal of the Corn Laws turned them into policy reality. 'Even today it is eerie how much he understood and how much he got right.'

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on the comparative advantage example: 'Should Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma drive to work? Begin with the assumption that they're the best drivers in Bombay. Actually they're not, I am.'
Amit on Trump's mercantilism: 'I have never heard this idea in my whole life until one low IQ American president said it.'
Amit on the local manufacturer's plea for protection: 'See I'm crying, I'm an infant, protect me' — mocking the rhetorical posture of 'infant industry' protection.

Amit's worry after Ajay calls for tariff-free services trade: 'I agree one hundred percent, but I worry that if Donald Trump listens to this part of the episode, the lesson he will take is goods and services are equal — why should I put tariffs only on goods? I will also put tariffs on services, and it will be your fault, Ajay.'
Amit on Ajay's smile-on-camera attempt: 'No, that's a very cute but a girly smile. Show your teeth!' — followed by Ajay 'trying, trying.' A small affectionate moment of podcast craft about teeth.

Amit on the parallel between Indira Gandhi and Modi on economic protectionism: 'It's like one is a successor of the other in terms of bad economic thinking. In other ways, they are very, very, very different.'
Ajay on Trump-administration internal dissent: 'Even people within his own administration know he's bullshitting, but they have to either kowtow or stay shut.'
'The double thank you moment' — John Stossel's framing of voluntary exchange. Customer thanks barista for the coffee; barista thanks customer for the money.
Joan Robinson: 'Just because other countries put rocks on their harbour doesn't mean we have to put rocks on our harbour.' Used to debunk reciprocal tariffs.
'An eye for an eye leaves the whole world blind' — Ajay's Gandhian frame for the futility of trade-war retaliation.

Norman Angell, The Great Illusion (1909): the famously timed pre-WWI argument that economic interdependence had made war between major powers impossible. Cited as a cautionary tale against complacency about today's order.
Keynes (1919): 'In 1914, the inhabitant of London could order by telephone, sipping his morning tea, the various products of the whole earth.' Captures pre-WWI globalisation in one sentence.

'Lebensraum' (living space) — Hitler's doctrine, articulated in Mein Kampf (1925), that Germany needed eastward conquest to acquire natural resources. Amit and Ajay argue Smoot-Hawley reinforced its logic by foreclosing trade as an alternative.
Nitin Pai's rule: every 1% rise in GDP lifts roughly 2 million Indians out of poverty (originally 1 million; revised upward on better data).
The Economist (founded 1843) — still calls itself a newspaper, founded specifically to defend free trade in the era of Cobden's Anti-Corn Law League.
Richard Cobden and the 1846 repeal of the Corn Laws — a milestone victory for free trade in 19th-century Britain.
Friedrich List — 19th-century German economic nationalist, cited as the counter-current to Smith and Ricardo's free-trade consensus.
Alexander Hamilton — popularised the 'infant industry' argument in early America. Cited as Hamilton-the-mercantilist to Jefferson-the-freedom-guy.
Marx and Engels: 'National one-sidedness and narrow-mindedness become more and more impossible in a globalized world' — correct description, wrong analysis (class warfare, exploitation).
The Washington Consensus (1989) — the late-20th-century cross-ideological agreement on globalisation's benefits, foreshadowed here as the subject of the next episode.
Pax Britannica — Britain's 19th-century policing of the seas that allowed free trade to spread globally.

The Columbian Exchange — Amit reads from Peter Vanham: 'Europeans brought wheat, sugarcane, horses, cattle, and devastating diseases like smallpox to the Americas, while from the Americas they took maize, corn, potatoes, tomatoes, cocoa and more back to Europe, Africa and Asia.'
